speakeroldname: Hon. Jacques Flynn (Minisler of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE IN MOVEMENT TO MARKETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, authority has been provided for a continuation of assistance in the movement of Canadian coal. The previous orders in council providing this assistance expired on March 31 and have been succeeded by new orders passed on April 2.
The recent royal commission on coal, otherwise known as the Rand commission, recommended that steps be taken to assist Canadian coal, particularly in the maritimes, to find an increasing and stable market in the home area. Such a market should over a period replace the present dependence on a large scale, costly movement to Ontario. The commission made specific recommendations in respect to maritime coal which were designed to accomplish this purpose. However, the market situation has been altering rapidly and is presently in such a fluid condition that it is considered inadvisable to confine the measures of assistance by unduly restrictive provisions.
The assistance now provided is defined in the respective orders in council which are not restrictive in time. It is our intention to keep the situation under constant review and to make such changes, from time to time, in the orders in council as production and market developments may require. This flexibility will not only encourage the shift in market areas recommended by the royal commission; it will make such shift as easy as possible under the conditions as they may develop, with the lowest possible expenditure necessary to accomplish the main purpose. This purpose remains, as in the past, the maintenance of a reasonable level of employment in Canadian coal mines.
Specifically the new orders provide that the assistance to the mines in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick be widened to include payment of a subvention on all coal shipped. Provision is also made to encourage an increasing movement by rail from the mines to large consumers in Quebec and Ontario rather than by the expensive movement by water and transshipment.
In western Canada provision is made to continue the assistance on the movement of coking coal from mines in Alberta and British Columbia for export. This provision will permit a continuation of the existing export to Japan.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE IN MOVEMENT TO MARKETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the areas concerned will welcome the announcement made by the minister to the effect that the assistance to the movement of coal to certain markets, both domestic and export, will be continued. As the minister said, this is in accordance with some of the recommendations of the Rand commission. The minister also said the situation was under constant review as far as production and markets are concerned.
I feel there will be some disappointment in the Cape Breton area in that the minister has made no specific announcement in connection with the proposed closing of No. 16 colliery. Furthermore, we expected at this time that the minister would make some specific announcement with regard to a national policy on coal. Such a policy is lacking. This is only a temporary measure designed to take care of an interim situation, but gives no definite or permanent relief to the area and to the industry concerned.

subtopic: * CANAL CONSTRUCTION, LAKE SIMCOE   EFFECT ON FISHERIES
* CANAL CONSTRUCTION, LAKE SIMCOE   EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext: Has the Department of Fisheries given any consideration to the possible effect on the fisheries, through smelt and lamprey infestation, of building a canal into lake Simeoe; and, if so, what is the result of that consideration?

subtopic: * CANAL CONSTRUCTION, LAKE SIMCOE   EFFECT ON FISHERIES
speechtext:
The answer, Mr. Speaker, is yes; scientists of the Department of Fisheries were asked by the Department of Transport for their opinion on this matter.
There is already an open waterway from lake Ontario into lake Simeoe but there is no evidence of lamprey or smelt entering lake Simeoe through this waterway. This does not guarantee, however, that if another all water route was established from Georgian bay, lamprey and smelt would not succeed in reaching lake Simeoe. They would, however, still have the problem of establishing themselves. If lamprey did establish themselves they would undoubtedly have an adverse effect on the lake trout. In the case of smelts, this species would compete with other fish in the lake, but it has been demonstrated that smelts can provide a profitable fishery as well as serving as food for the other species.

Answer by: Mr. Chambers:
Under the present system officer cadets at the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean and Royal Roads attend the Royal Military College at Kingston for the last two years of college training. Le College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean was established in 1952. The first group of officer cadets from College Militaire Royal graduated into the services in 1957. One of the objectives of the college was to enable French speaking cadets to commence their training in their native language. In this it has been a notable success. The program is under continuous study to see whether improvements can be made.

Canada and the United States in efforts to eliminate oil pollution of waters of the great lakes. In the first place, to deal with the points as I remember them, both the scope and the details required under this legislation are appreciably wider

as contained in the bill than they were in the bill which was introduced in the house last session. The hon. member has only to look at the requirements contained in clause 4 to see the very great extent to which the financial implications and details now required are extended beyond what would have been required under the earlier bill. He has also only to look at the definition of "corporation" and the other provisions affecting that to see that the number of companies who will now have to report is greatly enlarged compared with the number that would have been required to report under Bill No. C-70 last year.
The reason for making the exemptions contained in the schedule is that we considered it was not good practice and not necessary to make companies which are already under a very heavy burden of statistical reporting enlarge the burden by reporting under this measure if we were satisfied that the kind of information they now report to other places is (a) approximately as complete in its detail and coverage as what would be required here and (b) already available to the government. We came to the conclusion that the classes of corporations outlined in the exemptions mentioned in the schedule do qualify under these headings, namely that they report in comparatively equal detail already and that the information so reported is available to the government.
Let us take particularly, for instance, those in paragraph 15 of the schedule, to which a good deal of attention has been devoted. I am sure hon. members will agree with me that if you stop to think of it you will realize that the railway companies and the telephone company referred to are under a very heavy burden of reporting to the board of transport commissioners under the provisions of the Railway Act. Every time a rate application comes up there is a vast volume of information that is required to be filed with the board of transport commissioners. I assure my hon. friends that there is really a very heavy burden of reporting already laid upon these companies.
So we asked ourselves the question, should we add to that the burden of reporting simply for the sake of securing information under this act rather than under some other heading, having in mind especially that the information so filed already under that other heading is already available to the government? We came to the conclusion that on those grounds the class of companies in head 15 of the schedule, as well as those in the first six heads of the schedule, should not be subject to the additional burden of having to report under this legislation.

As I say, when we come to any particular heading in the schedule I will be glad to have a look at it and if we should become satisfied that we are wrong and that either the kind of information we want is not available or it is already reported but is not available to the government, then we would be prepared to reconsider our decision as reflected in the schedule. However, I do hope that when hon. members come to that point they will give due weight to the fact of the already quite considerable, indeed very considerable, burden of reporting to which these companies are already subject.
To deal with the only other point that I recall being raised, it was that by virtue of this exemption in head 15 smaller telephone companies or other telephone companies are not going to have to report and that they might well be foreign controlled to a degree or in total. That is completely misconstruing the effect of the bill and the schedule. Every company in Canada, subject only to the revenue and asset lower limits contained in the schedule, is required to report unless it is exempted by the schedule.
The only telephone companies exempted by the schedule are those in respect of which returns are made to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada in pursuance of the Railway Act. The telephone companies which report to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada are exempt from reporting because we feel information of the type we want is already available. Telephone companies which do not report to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada will be required to file returns under this act. One way or the other, therefore, we feel we will have all the information we want to have in respect of telephone companies in Canada.

Since the discussion last night in which I was involved, I have found that the Railway Act contains a section in addition to that to which I referred last night-section 391, I think. But in connection with section 391 there is a suggestion, in fact there is a directive, that information provided by a company-a railway company, a telephone company, or an express company incorporated under the Railway Act-must give certain information to the board of transport commissioners. But that information is not available to the public in a way such as is contemplated-

Not schedule B of this act. To sum up, I understand that financial information is not to be available to a representative of the public on payment of one dollar going to a certain minister's office. That is true, I agree, as far as the public

Corporations and Labour Unions reports are concerned. But as to the type of company referred to in the schedule which we discussed last night, items 1 to 6, about which there are published reports, it seems to me incongruous to find that all these companies do provide public information with respect to profit and loss, the very thing which has to remain secret with respect to other corporations under this bill. But these same companies do not, as I understand it, provide the public with the same accessibility on payment of one dollar as this bill makes necessary for all other corporations across Canada.
I think, as I said last night, that this is a sham-that this is a half baked measure and one which has not been properly presented by the minister. As far as banks are concerned, since our debate last night I have found that under the Bank Act, section 113, there is an obligation for the banks of our country within 30 days of the annual general meeting to transmit to the minister a return showing the name and address-I emphasize the word "address"-of each director. I referred to this yesterday in connection particularly with companies incorporated under the Railway Act. Now what does "address" mean? It means anything. I said yesterday it could involve a box number. If a wealthy man could employ a secretary in Montreal, or even have one of those recording machines to say that his address was box so and so, Montreal, he might be able to give Montreal as an address though his nationality might be other than Canadian.
I admitted yesterday that I had not looked at the Railway Act as carefully as I should have, but no member can look at all these statutes. I felt the minister last night was not as familiar with some of these statutes as he should have been. I did not refer last night to section 391 of the Railway Act. Neither did the minister. But if he looks at subsection 3 of that section he will find it might be possible for the board of transport commissioners to obtain information additional to that described, but under certain conditions. Why should our major industries such as the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Bell Telephone Company and others have an easier way of satisfying the desire on the part of the government to obtain information about foreign shareholding content than is provided in this bill?
I did not refer very much to insurance companies, and trust and loan companies last evening, but with respect to such companies I find there is executive discretion here. I observe that the minister has wide powers to obtain from such companies information on a prescribed form which he is empowered to change from year to year. All of these people

Corporations and Labour Unions might be put in the position of providing carbon copies of the type of information that other small companies across Canada are asked for under this bill, but that has not been the practice.
The chief point I wish to present to the minister is that there is discrimination here. The big companies such as insurance and trust and loan companies, railway companies, telephone companies and others that have good, efficient and, I assume, well paid accounting staffs, could provide this information; but the minister is placing an obligation upon all the other companies described in this bill for the provision of information which, as I said yesterday and as the hon. member for Skeena also said, does not relate oranges to grapefruit under any statistical form.
If I were to say this bill is insincere I would be guilty of using an unparliamentary phrase, but allow me to say that it represents something which I do not think will be proceeded with to any extent following the next election. As I said yesterday, this is window dressing. I do not see that the measure is of much advantage to the country, especially when there is no harmony in the correlation of statistical information.

A moment ago the minister said again-he has said this a number of times; he said it in reply to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River-that it was the desire of the government, as I gathered his words, to get information about the operation of the Canadian economy; that this was most necessary for the government in order to be able to deal with the economy; that they want the facts, the true facts, all the facts and the precise facts. This is what I understand is the desire of the government.
All we need to do is to balance that statement against the bill before us which is not designed to get all the facts but only some of the facts and which is not designed to get all of the information but only some of the information, and to balance that statement made by the minister just a moment ago against his attitude and the attitude of his government when the Combines Investigation Act was being considered by this parliament and by the banking and commerce committee. The effect of the whole discussion is quite clear in the statute itself, Mr. Chairman. I mentioned the matter only in passing because of the statement now made by the minister that he wishes to get that information. I say that all we have to do is to balance this statement against the bill and against what he said a couple of years ago on the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. If we do so, we shall see that they do not balance. What the minister and the government do is oftentimes quite different-and it certainly is different in this case-from what they say.
The minister made a speech to the Canadian petroleum industry on February 22, in Regina. In that speech he made reference to this particular bill. In one of his comments there- and if I may do so I will read it-he said this:
The intent of this bill is to make known the precise degree of foreign control over Canadian corporations and unions.
He has used this word "precise" on a number of occasions. Sometimes he says "somewhat precise"; sometimes he says "almost precise" or "similar". To me there is some distinction between "precise", "almost precise" and "similar". From that I take it that he was not misleading the Canadian petroleum association meeting in Regina but that he was telling them precisely what he wanted to know, namely the precise degree of foreign control over Canadian corporations and unions. However, this is not what the bill seeks to do. The bill seeks to get some information from some companies or corporations, as they are called in the bill. It seeks to get some information by way of this bill. It seeks to get other information from other types of corporations by way of other acts which are already in existence. It is certainly not the same information. The minister says that he can relate the information statistically and come up with some information. However, when we analyse the information carefully, I think we will find that it is not designed to get an understanding of the precise degree of foreign control or to get full information as to the operation of the whole Canadian economy, as there are other matters that are certainly known. The minister also placed these statistics on record. It is true that they were given in a general way. The hon. member for Leeds made reference

Corporations and Labour Unions to them, others have made reference to them and I made reference to them. I refer to the dominion bureau of statistics figures with regard to the degree of foreign control over sections of our economy.
The dominion bureau of statistics now determines, as it has been doing for some years, what is the degree of foreign control that exists over Canadian industry in the manufacturing field. That information was placed on the record. As of 1959, it was 57 per cent and it has been increasing. They have information about the petroleum and natural gas industry. In Regina on February 22 the minister told the Canadian petroleum association that the figure was approximately 75 per cent. The dominion bureau of statistics says as far as they are concerned it is 75 per cent. Information about the mining industry has been placed on the record and an analysis by the dominion bureau of statistics of the degree of the control over the Canadian industry. There is information not only about the degree of foreign control but about the degree of foreign ownership. This gives a different figure percentagewise because it adds up different bits of information. This is information which the dominion bureau of statistics has. It is available. It is a public document. How does the dominion bureau of statistics get this information? How does d.b.s. now know this and how is it able to say and to report publicly that in 1959, with respect to the mining, petroleum and natural gas manufacturing industry, the degree of foreign control over that industry was 63 per cent. How do d.b.s. know this? How do they know that this control increased in the last two years from 61 per cent? How do they know it has increased in the last five years by some 8 per cent? How do the dominion bureau of statistics get this information? Do they guess it? Do they search through information which is filed with them? Do they look through the annual reports of various companies and then say, "This is what we discover about the degree of ownership and about the degree of control"?
I think the minister, even though he is not the Minister of Trade and Commerce, owes us an explanation as to how the dominion bureau of statistics obtain the information which allows them to make the statement that there is over certain sections of our economy at the moment this degree of control which the minister blessed by making reference to it himself in the house. I think this is some information which the committee needs to have before we can proceed to determine whether or not it is really worth while to pass the bill at present before us. If this information is knowledgeable-as apparently it is, to d.b.s.-how accurate it is, I do not


know-surely that consideration may affect our decision with respect to other features of the bill as to just what type of information is required to be filed at the moment. Is this a case in which they take from public corporations any financial statements they issue or is this information which they have already gleaned in one way or another by way of statistics which are required to be filed with them?
I do not wish to be overly insistent about this matter. However, I think it is a rather important point. Apparently d.b.s. now get some statistical information. Otherwise they would not be able to come up with the statement that 63 per cent of the industry in Canada is under foreign control at the moment. We should like to know how d.b.s. get this information, what statistics are filed with them, from what sorts of corporations, or whether this is an accurate or inaccurate figure. I take it that corporations such as General Motors, which is a private company, are left outside the analysis that the bureau of statistics makes of manufacturing industries. The minister also referred to Canadian General Electric and two or three other corporations which are very large private companies that do not file information now. If these companies are outside of the area surveyed by the bureau of statistics in coming to the conclusion that the manufacturing industry of Canada is 57 per cent foreign owned, I think we are entitled to come to the conclusion that this figure is too low and should be increased in order to be more correct.
This is information which I for one would like to have from the minister so that we can assess, first, the value which we should place upon the figures already published by d.b.s. and, second, the value which we should place upon each of the provisions in section 4 asking for specific items of information. We should atempt to determine whether we really require the information requested in the bill or whether it is already being supplied in some other form. If the minister can assist the committee in this way it may help us to proceed with the consideration of the bill more speedily.

Mr. Chairman, before we go too far astray I wonder whether I might point out that, while I am anxious to co-operate with the committee and to give as much information as is relevant, the kind of speech we have heard in the last three quarters of an hour has really been the kind of speech that would be made on second or third reading when the principle of the bill is under discussion. Indeed, one hon. member used the phrase "before deciding whether or not to pass the bill I want to know" this, that or the other thing. May I point out that we are not deciding whether to pass the bill. We are dealing with the clauses of the bill because the bill was given second reading the day before yesterday. We have passed clause 1 where general discussion is by custom permitted and there was a wide ranging general discussion at that time. We are now on clause 3.
I have forborne raising this point before because I want to co-operate with the committee, but when we have the kind of speech made just now by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River then I say we are definitely engaging in a second reading type of discussion. I do not want to appear omniscient when I say this but I can assure the committee that all the points that have been raised so far were considered and that while they are all very difficult we came to the conclusion that to accomplish the object we had in mind this was the best way of doing it.
Now, with regard to the question of statistics that are compiled by the dominion bureau and published, I can refer the committee to the recent report on the Canadian balance of international payments in 1960 and the international investment position, page 62, where the bureau itself has fully set out a summary of the methods it follows in compiling these statistics and makes an assessment of their accuracy and reliability.
In so far as the question of whether or not this may open the door to raiding is concerned, I can say I certainly think it will not. It will have the opposite effect and will enable Canadians, by their increased knowledge of the affairs of these companies and the increased information available about them, more effectively to get into a position where they can participate in the direction of these companies and the

Corporations and Labour Unions benefits from them. I would remind the committee in that connection that it was this government which early in our period of responsibility, when the threat of a takeover of some quite substantial Canadian life insurance companies did develop, acted to fill the gap that had been there for so long. This provision allowed insurance companies to take steps towards mutualization which would make it impossible for these companies to be taken over.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of the creation of a water pollution control division, composed of representatives of the ten provinces, within the framework of the proposed national resources council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate, and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces: in addition, to further the study of water pollution control problems of a national character.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this motion today I am making an appeal which has nothing to do with political beliefs or partisan convictions. The members of this party are alarmed at the sight of our industries and people polluting our waters, as it were, with their own hands from day to day. All over many parts of Canada the water table is falling, yet thousands of factories and hundreds of municipal sewer systems are discharging their wastes into our rivers and lakes with only a small fraction of our industries or municipalities giving so-called adequate treatment to this increasing flow of filth.
We all know that water is the lifeblood of any country and, while in the last 20 years 26207-1-160J

I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the soul of man, shaken and bruised by the ceaseless din of modern cities, which some people worship-and I am one who does not-and the relentless international and national sabre rattling, in this atmosphere more than ever, I believe, needs treeways rather than freeways, and pure waterways rather than sewerways.
However, regardless of these needs we continue to disfigure the natural landscape, erode our soils, destroy our forests and pollute our waters, in some cases almost with the zeal of a religious mission. It is because of the gruesome proof of the shortcomings of our legislation both federal and provincial, and the determination of this party to do all it can within its sphere of influence in the House of Commons and in the country to remedy this field, that I bring this resolution before the house this afternoon.
Strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, the problem of pollution has been recognized officially by both federal and provincial governments -I am speaking now of the federal parliament and the provincial government of British Columbia-since 1870, and it has been recognized that some form of legislation is required. We can even read debates of that date which clearly indicate that people were concerned about this matter in 1870. If they were concerned at that time, or at least some people were, how much more concerned should we be today? Yet since that time, except for some federal legislation of a bits and bobs nature leaving the responsibility with various departments of the federal government, and some provincial legislation of the same nature leaving the responsibility with numerous departments, in most provinces there has been little effective action, because all that has been done has been on a piecemeal basis. So that while the problem has been recognized for all these years and there has been legislation in part to meet it, we find that even a river such as the Ottawa is termed by most of the people of this city as a flowing sewer. We have heard the Prime Minister deal with the pollution of the Saskatchewan river, and I know something about the increasing pollution of the great Fraser river in British Columbia and something about the very limited but none the less real pollution occurring in the Kootenay and Columbia rivers.

But still the problem is increasing from day to day and pollution is greater in this country with every 24 hours that pass.
What we require, in the opinion of this party, is first of all a knowledge of the situation on a national basis. Then we need an understanding of the problem, an understanding on the part of our people. Strangely enough this is a problem which is not very glamourous. It is similar to the problem of the conservation of timber or the conservation of land; it does not strike the imagination of many people and very often it does not strike the imagination of the press. I noticed that in the press today there is considerable comment on the possibility of a divorce of two prominent movie people. This matter has been given far too much space in the newspapers, and they would be far better off if they reported fully my speech this afternoon, Mr. Speaker.
There has to be understanding on the part of the people and there has to be co-operation among federal and provincial governments, the local authorities and the people. This type of program is just the same as a forestry or a land conservation program; governments alone cannot give effect to it; there must be the understanding and cooperation of a large percentage of the population in the area in which the program is being implemented.
Throughout the years I have subscribed to the minutes of the British Columbia natural resources conference which is held annually in Victoria, Vancouver or somewhere else in British Columbia, to which go representatives of industry, labour, universities and government and discuss the various questions related to natural resources. In this connection I wish to quote very briefly from the sixth British Columbia natural resources conference which deals quite extensively with the question of water pollution. I wish to read one paragraph which has to do with the effectiveness of the present legislation. This is what the writer has to say:
Considering the objectives for which they have been enacted, the various items of legislation have 

had considerable effect on the prevention and control of certain types of pollution. However, since the control has been carried out by separate government agencies, each with its own interest to consider, sometimes co-operating with other agencies and sometimes not,-
That is the situation today; there is duplication, overlapping.
-the existing legislation probably has not been as effective in controlling pollution in all its aspects as it might have been.
That paragraph was written by a civil servant in British Columbia, and of course he had to place the situation before the conference in modest terms; but a lot more can be read into his words than appears on the surface. However, he goes on to deal with the various departments which have to deal with this matter. As far as British Columbia is concerned, we have these government agencies responsible for dealing with water pollution: local boards of health, the health branch of the department of health and welfare, the water rights branch of the department of lands and forests, the park service of the department of lands and forests, the fisheries department, the game commission, the attorney general's department; and we have the health act of British Columbia, the sanitary regulations of British Columbia, section 58 of the municipal act, the watershed regulations, the water act and the park regulations. They all deal with the various aspects of the pollution of waters.
As far as the federal government is concerned, we have the Department of Fisheries which administers the Fisheries Act and which deals with the pollution of waters, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources which deals with the Migratory Birds Convention Act, the national harbours board which deals with harbours by-laws, the Department of Transport dealing with the Navigable Waters Protection Act and the Canada Shipping Act, the Department of Public Works, and the local port authorities of the Department of Transport dealing with ports under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. So we have quite a body of legislation in the federal and provincial fields.
There is a good deal of legislation in both the federal and the provincial fields but in neither of these fields has there been a great deal of co-operation, and there has not been the co-ordinated approach to this problem which is necessary if we are to meet it.
This subject was the subject of a number of papers at the resources for tomorrow conference. The minister was good enough to send me a report of this conference and I found it very interesting reading when I had any spare time, though you will understand, Mr. Speaker, that I have very little time in present circumstances for meditation or for

reading other than resolutions and legislation and the letters that I get from people. I get a very large fan mail. However, I took an interest in reading this report and I have read the papers on water pollution in Canada.
I wish simply to quote from the concluding paragraph because it supports my contention. As a matter of fact, it prompted me to introduce this motion this afternoon in the form in which I did introduce it. On page 359 of the report, I read this-it comes at the conclusion of a lengthy paper on water pollution in Canada:
Possibly the greatest present need is a better knowledge of pollution problems on the part of the taxpayer. So many demands are being made for increased expenditures in urban communities that sewage treatment gets little support in many areas.
In summary, pollution problems of major significance are already evident in Canada and will become more common and more severe as industrial and urban development increases. Hence, a more complete knowledge of present conditions coupled with prompt and effective remedial action, is essential for future national development and expansion.
I am confident that this effective remedial action cannot take place unless there is a coordinated approach to research and study followed by co-operation between governments and government agencies to give it effect. The first essential is knowledge based on research-an over-all knowledge of the situation as it exists in Canada. We have a great body of knowledge which is already available, or would be available if it were coordinated and presented to a central committee such as I suggest composed of persons representing the federal and provincial governments. Then we must have co-operation between governments and co-operation between the government agencies concerned. Following that we need a redrafting of legislation. It will mean a reallocation of responsibility for dealing with certain areas of this problem and also the education of the public to support the raising of the funds which will be necessary to meet the situation. It will mean taxes in municipal areas. It will mean, possibly, some particular taxation on a provincial basis and on a national basis. I believe this should be in the nature of taxation for a specific purpose, especially in the provinces; people in the provinces should know that there is a cent, or whatever it is, of their sales tax going to meet the pollution problems in their region. I think there would then be a better understanding of the problem. Anyway, there is room for education in this respect.
I wish to give other hon. members an opportunity to speak on this subject, but before ending my remarks let me say it cannot be overemphasized that damage to the natural

An exterminated species cannot be revived; a stand of virgin timber can never be replaced in its virgin form, and polluted waters can never be returned to their original purity. Another problem which contributes to water pollution is the fact that a great many of the cities through which these rivers flow have inadequate sewage disposal facilities. Indeed, in the city of Winnipeg itself my understanding is that the sewage disposal facilities are completely inadequate and out-dated and that the method of treatment of the sewage is not what it should be today. A first step in that educational program would be to educate the public to an acceptance of the fact that only through taxation of some form, only through money provided by the people, will this problem be controlled. It affects wildlife around our coast, particularly bird life.
It probably has some effect on the fisheries. I realize that the Department of Transport has a certain division that does something in this respect involving the working out of agreements with other countries, but in spite of this we do not seem to be coping with the problem very well. Every year there is more and more evidence of bird life being destroyed by oil dumped outside our territorial waters which drifts in toward the shore, or in some cases by oil that is dumped within our own coastal waters.

The house leader did leave me a note, the contents of which he asked me to communicate to the house. It is that the No. 1 item will be interim supply-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the first item?
The first item, yes; No. 2 will be Bill No. C-38 and No. 3 will be supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I asked about Friday as well. Do I take it it will be a continuation of this? What is the business for Friday?
All I have is what I have given. I think this will be the order-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For tomorrow?
Yes.
It being three minutes past six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, April 5, 1962
